title: La Silla dawn kisses the Milky Way
caption: The Milky Way at dawn over La Silla Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at La Silla Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Just before dawn at La Silla Observatory, an orange layer hovers over the horizon, signaling that the Sun is about to rise. Above it, the Milky Way stretches across the entire sky, dotted with dark patches where dust particles block light from behind. In the foreground stand several of the observatory's telescopes.

Closest to the camera is the Swedish–ESO Submillimeter Telescope (SEST), with a dish 15 meters across. It was retired in 2003, its work taken over by APEX and ALMA. On the plateau behind stand the ESO 3.6-meter telescope and, just beyond it, the Coudé Auxiliary Telescope.

SEST seems to point at a dazzling object. That is Venus, lit by the Sun and brighter than any star in the night sky. Rising from the horizon through Venus is a triangular white glow called zodiacal light, which is sunlight scattered by dust lying in the ecliptic, the plane of Earth's orbit around the Sun.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph credited to ESO/B. Tafreshi. The source does not publish camera, exposure or color-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light over time, so the faint zodiacal light and the Milky Way may look more pronounced here than to someone standing at the site.

explore: La Silla lies on the outskirts of the Chilean Atacama Desert. The two facilities that took over from SEST are the Atacama Pathfinder EXperiment telescope and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array.
alt: Telescopes under a pre-dawn sky with an orange glow on the horizon, the Milky Way overhead, and bright Venus inside a faint triangular glow.
